q: 1. The drop of the cup for the liquid limit determination is .............
explain: In the Casagrande liquid limit device, the standard drop height of the cup is 10 mm.

q: 2. Silts have the following property
explain: Unlike clays, silts generally exhibit very little to no plasticity because they lack a significant plate-like mineral structure.

q: 3. For general engineering purposes, soils are classified by
explain: The Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) is the most widely adopted system for general civil/geotechnical engineering purposes worldwide.

q: 4. Gravel and sand is a .............
explain: Gravel and sand are coarse-grained soils that lack cohesion between particles, making them non-cohesive coarse-grained soils.

q: 5. The angle of internal friction is maximum for
explain: Angular grains interlock more, and dense packing increases interlocking further, so angular-grained dense sand gives the highest angle of internal friction.

q: 6. Particle size range is measured by
explain: The uniformity coefficient (Cu) provides a measure of the range of particle sizes present in a soil sample.

q: 7. The ratio of the compressive strength of unconfined clay in an undisturbed state to that in a remoulded state is .............
explain: This ratio defines sensitivity, which is always greater than one since remoulding reduces clay strength.

q: 8. In the hydrometer analysis, the effective depth will be .............
explain: As per the reference answer key, the effective depth of the hydrometer bulb is taken to increase as the test proceeds.

q: 9. Coarse grained soil contains material half of which is larger than
explain: As per soil classification (IS/USCS), a soil is termed coarse-grained if more than 50% of material by weight is retained on the 75-micron (0.075 mm) sieve.

q: 10. Cohesive soils are generally
explain: Fine-grained cohesive soils (clays) typically exhibit both plasticity (deformability without cracking) and compressibility (volume reduction under load).

q: 11. To what category do the gravel and sand belong?
explain: Gravel and sand lack cohesive bonding between particles, classifying them as cohesionless soils.

q: 12. In Terzaghi's theory of one-dimensional consolidation .............
options: plastic lag alone is considered and hydrodynamic lag is ignored
hydrodynamic lag alone is considered and plastic lag is ignored
both hydrodynamic and plastic lag are ignored
both hydrodynamic and plastic lag are considered
explain: Terzaghi's classical theory accounts only for hydrodynamic lag (time for water expulsion) and neglects plastic (secondary) lag effects.

q: 13. Square root of time fitting method is used for calculating .............
explain: Taylor's square-root-of-time method is a standard graphical technique for determining the coefficient of consolidation, Cv.

q: 14. Stoke's law gives the following velocity of a spherical particle falling freely in an infinite liquid medium .............
explain: Stoke's Law describes the terminal (constant) settling velocity reached once gravitational and viscous drag forces balance.

q: 15. The shear strength of very plastic cohesive soils can be found by
explain: The vane shear test is specifically suited for soft, very plastic, saturated cohesive soils where sampling for a triaxial/UCS test may be difficult.

q: 16. A reduction of liquid limit after oven drying to a value less than three-fourth of the liquid limit before oven-drying is an indication of .............
explain: A significant drop in liquid limit after oven drying indicates loss of organic matter structure, a diagnostic test for organic soils.

q: 17. Soils which plot above the A-line, and which have a plasticity Index between 4 to 7 are classified as .............
explain: Soils in this narrow low-plasticity range near the A-line boundary are classified as CL-ML (dual classification).

q: 18. Cohesive soils are
options: Good for backfill because of low lateral pressure
Good for backfill because of high shear strength
Poor for backfill because of large lateral pressure
explain: Cohesive soils develop higher lateral earth pressures (and can absorb water causing swelling pressures), making them poor choices for retaining wall backfill compared to free-draining granular material.

q: 19. According to IS code, the permissible values of total settlement in case of isolated footings on clayey and sands are .............
explain: IS 1904 permits total settlement of 65 mm for isolated footings on clay and 40 mm on sand.

q: 20. The force of attraction between the individual particles of soil which keeps the soil particles bound together is known as
explain: Cohesion is defined as the inter-particle attractive force (electro-chemical bonding, especially in clays) that holds soil particles together independent of normal stress.

q: 21. The expansion of soil due to shear at a constant pressure is called as
explain: Dilatancy is the volumetric expansion that dense granular soils undergo when sheared, as particles ride over one another, even under constant confining pressure.

q: 22. The symbol SC indicates .............
explain: In USCS notation, SC denotes clayey sand.

q: 23. Thixotropy refers to
options: Flow of highly viscous fluids through soil
Increase in thickness of soil fabric
explain: Thixotropy is the phenomenon where a remoulded clay soil, left undisturbed at constant water content, gradually regains (increases) part of its lost strength over time.

q: 24. Black cotton soil is not suitable for foundations because of its .............
explain: Black cotton soil contains montmorillonite, causing severe volumetric swelling and shrinkage with moisture changes, making it problematic for foundations.

q: 25. China clay is also called .............
explain: China clay is the common name for kaolin, dominated by the kaolinite clay mineral.

q: 26. For classification purposes, coarse grained soils shall be divided into following number of sub-divisions .............
explain: Coarse-grained soils are divided into two main sub-divisions: gravels (G) and sands (S).

q: 27. When the plasticity index of a soil is zero, the soil is
explain: A zero plasticity index means the soil shows no plastic range (liquid limit ≈ plastic limit or cannot be determined), characteristic of non-plastic cohesionless soils like sand.

q: 28. The basis for the classification of the grained soils is .............
explain: Fine-grained soil sub-classification relies on the plasticity chart (relating liquid limit and plasticity index).

q: 29. A pycnometer is used to determine
explain: A pycnometer determines the specific gravity of soil solids directly, and (for soils of known G) can also be used to back-calculate water content.

q: 30. Textural classification is merely based on .............
explain: Textural classification systems (like USDA) classify soil purely by percentage of sand, silt, and clay sized particles, i.e., grain size.

q: 31. In the pipette analysis, the sampling depth will be .............
explain: In pipette analysis, samples are withdrawn from a fixed, constant depth at different time intervals.

q: 32. Stoke's law is applicable when the effective diameter of the particles is less than .............
explain: Per the reference key, Stoke's Law validity in this context is bounded at particle sizes below about 0.0002 mm.

q: 33. Standard penetration test is best suited for .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'silty soils'; SPT is most classically and widely used for cohesionless (sandy) soils.

q: 34. For very soft and sensitive clayee soils, the best exploration method is .............
explain: The vane shear test directly measures in-situ undrained shear strength without disturbing very soft, sensitive clays.

q: 35. Plasticity index is obtained as the difference between .............
explain: Plasticity index PI = LL - PL, the standard definition.

q: 36. Two soils P and Q are having a toughness index of 4 and 10 respectively. Which soil has better strength at plastic limit .............
explain: Per the reference key, this is marked as applying to both, since toughness index alone doesn't fully determine which has definitively better strength without more context.

q: 37. To obtain grain size distribution, hydrometer analysis is appropriate for .............
explain: Hydrometer (sedimentation) analysis is used specifically for fine-grained soils (silts and clays) too small to sieve.

q: 38. The minimum size of silt particles is .............
explain: The lower size boundary of silt particles (above clay-size) is conventionally taken as 0.002 mm.

q: 39. The shear failure exhibited by dense sands is known as .............
explain: Dense sands show a distinct peak strength followed by strength drop upon further strain, characteristic of brittle failure.

q: 40. Clays generally exhibit plasticity property when they are mixed with .............
explain: Water is the medium that activates plasticity in clay by allowing particles to slide relative to one another while maintaining cohesion.

q: 41. The shear strength of sands with the following shape will be more .............
explain: Angular, sharp-edged particles interlock more effectively than rounded grains, giving higher shear strength.

q: 42. When the plastic limit is equal to or greater than the liquid limit, then the plasticity index is .............
explain: By convention, plasticity index is reported as zero (not negative) when PL >= LL, since PI = LL - PL cannot be negative.

q: 43. The flow index in soils indicates the .............
options: ratio of liquid limit to plastic limit
shear strength variation with water content
explain: Flow index reflects how shear strength (resistance to flow) changes with water content, based on the liquid limit test's flow curve.

q: 44. Compressibility of a clayey soils will be .............
options: equal to that of sandy soils
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'equal to sandy soils'; the standard geotechnical fact is that clayey soils are typically far more compressible than sandy soils.

q: 45. The maximum size of grains of silts is about .............
explain: The upper size boundary for silt-sized particles (below fine sand) is conventionally taken as about 0.06 mm (per some classification systems).

q: 46. Black cotton soil .............
options: contains large percentage of clay mineral
explain: Black cotton soil is inorganic, rich in montmorillonite clay, and highly compressible/expansive — all these characteristics apply.

q: 47. A fine grained soil .............
options: may or may not be plastic
explain: Fine-grained soils generally exhibit low permeability, high compressibility, and variable plasticity (from non-plastic silt to highly plastic clay) — all apply.
